system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 6 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2134-09-08 20:58:00 to 2134-09-14 14:45:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 65-year-old male with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, coronary artery disease, and type 2 diabetes was admitted for left-sided chest pain associated with severe hyperkalemia (potassium 7.1) and EKG changes. He received emergency treatment with calcium gluconate and underwent emergent hemodialysis, which improved his symptoms and normalized potassium. Serial troponins were stable, ruling out acute myocardial infarction. He remained chest pain-free, completed a second dialysis session, and was discharged home in stable condition. The rise in potassium was not clearly due to dietary indiscretion; nephrology will evaluate for underlying causes such as hypoaldosteronism. Medications were adjusted, including increasing lisinopril and adding docusate, and low-potassium diet counseling was provided.
problems: Diabetes with renal manifestations, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled

.
You were found to have a urinary tract infection and hematuria.  
We recommend that you complete your course of antibiotics and 
follow up with Urology for possible cystocopy.
.
You mentioned that you were concerned about a chronic ulceration 
at the tip of your toe.  We recommend that you see you 
podiatrist within the next 2weeks.  We have contacted your 
podiatrist and their office should be calling you with an 
appointment.  
.
If you develop chest pain, shortness of breath, palpitations, or 
any other concerning symptom, please contact your doctor or go 
to the emergency room.
.
Please take all your medications as prescribed and follow up 
with the appointments below.
.
We have the following changes to your medications: 
We have increased your dose of lisinopril to 40mg by mouth 
daily.
We have increased your metoprolol to 25mg by mouth twice daily. 
We will prescribe you Ciprofloxacin 500mg by mouth daily to 
complete the treatement for your urinary tract infection. 

Please continue taking your other medications as prescribe 
including your aspirin and plavix. 
 
Followup Instructions:
___

procedures.long_title: Insertion of drug-eluting coronary artery stent(s)

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. Johnson. I'm Dr. Patel. I understand you came in with chest pain after dinner tonight?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. It's right here in the middle, under my breastbone. It’s been there for about two hours now. Didn’t go away with nitroglycerin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Did it radiate anywhere? Any nausea or sweating?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just nausea once. No radiation. But I’ve been really stressed lately—my dialysis schedule changed because of the holidays, and it’s been hard to keep up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. We’ve checked your EKG and your troponin levels—no signs of a heart attack so far. But given your history, we need to be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had this before. Last time, it got better after dialysis. Do you think it’s related?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Your blood pressure is high tonight, and your exam shows some fluid overload. We’ll keep monitoring you and may schedule an extra dialysis session.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. But the pain’s still here. Is it safe to wait?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve given you morphine, which helped a bit. That suggests it’s cardiac in origin. We’re not ruling anything out. Tomorrow, you’ll have a stress test to check for blockages.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. I just want to make sure nothing’s missed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are stable. Creatinine is high, as expected, but potassium is normal. We’re going ahead with the stress test today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it be safe with my heart history?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s a monitored test. They’ll watch your EKG closely. The goal is to see if your heart gets enough blood when it’s working harder.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well on the test. You developed chest pain during recovery, but no EKG changes. That’s concerning because it suggests possible angina, but we can’t confirm without imaging.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given your risk factors and persistent symptoms, we’re recommending a cardiac catheterization. It will let us see your arteries directly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that a surgery?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s a procedure. A small tube goes through your groin to your heart. We’ll inject dye to see any blockages. If we find one, we may place a stent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you. When will it happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Tomorrow morning. We’ll also schedule an extra dialysis session to help with fluid balance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your dialysis went well this morning. You’re feeling less bloated?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, my legs feel lighter. But the chest pain came back last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We saw that in the notes. That’s why the cath is even more important. We’ll proceed as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Mr. Johnson. You’re back from the cath lab. Everything went well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Did you find anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. You have two-vessel disease, but your bypass grafts are still open. We found a blockage in the LAD artery and placed a drug-eluting stent. We also did angioplasty to open it up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that should help the chest pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we’ll keep you on Plavix and aspirin to prevent clots. Your pain should improve now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve been worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also noticed something else—your urine test showed blood, and your hemoglobin dropped a bit. We gave you a transfusion yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hematuria? Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t know the cause yet. The urine culture was negative, so no infection. But we’re starting you on antibiotics just in case and recommending a urology follow-up for a cystoscopy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve also been meaning to ask—my toe ulcer hasn’t healed. Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we noted that. Given your vascular history, it’s important. We’ve contacted your podiatrist. They’ll call you for an appointment in the next two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ve been trying to keep it clean.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood pressure has been high, so we’ve increased your lisinopril to 40 mg daily. We also increased your metoprolol to help with heart rate and BP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been on lisinopril before. Is it safe with my kidneys?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we adjust the dose for kidney function. It actually helps protect your kidneys over time, especially with diabetes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright. And the new antibiotic?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Ciprofloxacin—for four days. It’s precautionary. Even though the culture was negative, we want to cover all bases with the hematuria.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—we’re discharging you today. You’re stable, euvolemic, and your chest pain is gone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take all your medications as listed. Especially aspirin and Plavix—don’t stop them. The nitroglycerin is for chest pain—use it as directed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the cipro?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Finish all four pills. And follow up with urology and podiatry. If you have chest pain, shortness of breath, or leg swelling, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll also send records to your primary doctor. Keep your appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—should I avoid salt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, absolutely. No added salt. It helps with fluid and blood pressure. Your dietitian can give you more tips.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll be careful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done well. Just keep up with your dialysis and follow-ups. You’re going home in good shape.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll have a nurse go over your discharge instructions one more time before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care, Mr. Johnson. Stay well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in before discharge. Any new symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, still feeling good. Chest is clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll finalize your paperwork. You should be out by noon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—we did an ultrasound on your groin after the cath. Everything looks good—no bleeding or clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Glad to hear it. I was a little worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Normal follow-up. You’re all set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks for explaining everything so clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. That’s our job. Take it easy at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you at follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, or sooner if needed. Here’s my number if anything comes up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate it. I’ll keep it handy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Alright, Mr. Johnson. You’re officially discharged. Take care.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 65-year-old male with end-stage renal disease on hemodialysis, coronary artery disease, and diabetes was admitted for persistent substernal chest pain unresponsive to nitroglycerin. Initial evaluation showed no EKG changes or troponin elevation, but due to high cardiac risk and ongoing symptoms, he underwent an exercise stress test that revealed reduced exercise tolerance and symptoms during recovery. A cardiac catheterization confirmed two-vessel coronary disease with a significant blockage in the LAD, leading to placement of a drug-eluting stent and PTCA. He also received an extra hemodialysis session for volume overload and was transfused for anemia. A urinary tract infection with hematuria was treated with antibiotics, and outpatient urology and podiatry follow-ups were arranged for hematuria and a chronic toe ulcer. Blood pressure was managed with uptitrated lisinopril and metoprolol. He was discharged home in stable condition with updated medications and clear follow-up instructions.
